Yes — it is coherent, though only on some theories of harm.

A good way to argue for this is to reject the idea that harm must always consist in a bad experience felt by the person at the time it occurs. If that were true, then death would make all later events morally irrelevant to the dead, because the dead have no consciousness. But many harms we already recognize are not best understood as unpleasant experiences. A person can be harmed by betrayal, deception, or humiliation even if they never discover it. If a friend steals from me but I die before learning of it, it still seems true that I was wronged and, in an important sense, harmed. The badness lies not in my felt suffering but in the defeat of my interests.

On this view, a person has interests that extend beyond the moment-to-moment contents of consciousness. I may care about whether my children flourish after I die, whether my body is treated with respect, whether my papers are published, or whether promises made to me are kept. These are not just present desires for certain feelings; they are projects and commitments that partly constitute my life. To frustrate them after my death is to make my life go worse than it otherwise would have gone. The harm is “posthumous” only in timing; what is damaged is the person’s life as a whole, considered as a temporally extended narrative.

This position does not require spooky metaphysics. We need not imagine a dead person somewhere undergoing injury. We can instead say: an event after death can stand in a relation of setback to interests the person had while alive. That is enough to make “posthumous harm” intelligible. The person is not harmed as a current subject of experience, but as the bearer of a life whose aims and values can still be honored or defeated.

An obvious objection comes from timing: when exactly is the person harmed? Not before the event, because it has not happened yet; not after, because the person no longer exists. But this objection may demand too much precision. We often identify harms by their relation to a person’s good, not by locating a mysterious metaphysical instant at which the damage “lands.” If my reputation is secretly destroyed today though I never learn of it, I am harmed even if no phenomenological change occurs in me. Similarly, posthumous events can alter whether a person’s life was successful on its own terms.

Still, the view needs limits. Not everything done after death harms the dead. If my trivial preference about what song should be played at a memorial is ignored, it may be a slight, but perhaps not a genuine harm unless that preference was important to my values or identity. Also, the interests of the living can override the dead’s interests. A promise to conceal evidence of a crime should not be kept merely because the dead wanted it. So posthumous harm is real, but not absolute.

What follows for wills? Wills make especially good sense on this account. If people can be harmed by the frustration of their surviving interests, then there is moral reason — not merely legal convenience — to respect testamentary instructions. Violating a will can wrong and harm the deceased by defeating serious projects they set for the future of their property, family, or legacy. But because the dead no longer participate in social life as full claimants, their interests should not necessarily have unlimited force. The law is right to impose restrictions: forced heirship rules, public-policy exceptions, limits on dead-hand control, and doctrines against unreasonable conditions all reflect the fact that the living also matter. Respect the will, but not at any cost.

The same applies to posthumous reputation. Slandering the dead can be morally serious even if the dead feel nothing, because reputation is often one of the goods people care deeply about as part of the meaning of their lives. To maliciously destroy someone’s name after death may therefore harm them in the sense just described. It also harms the living — families, historians, communities, and public trust. However, concern for posthumous reputation must be balanced against truth. We should not protect the dead from accurate criticism merely because it damages their image. The right implication is not “never speak ill of the dead,” but rather “do not falsely or gratuitously deform the shape of a person’s life.”

So the most defensible position is: yes, the dead can be harmed by later events, if harm is understood as a setback to enduring interests rather than as experienced suffering. That supports substantial respect for wills and for posthumous reputation, while still allowing the claims of truth, justice, and the welfare of the living to override the wishes of the dead in some cases.
